briefs.headline: NRI woman’s FCNR deposits get tax notice as unexplained; ITAT grants relief
briefs.deck: A woman, who originally hails from Beawar, and now resides in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE), decided to put money into investments in India. She along with her husband invested Rs 3.41 crore in two Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) term deposits. The husband’s name appeared as the first holder of both deposits, with the woman listed as the second holder.
briefs.bodyText:
Indians based globally and investing in India can in some cases face tax notices for unexplained income.
In one such case, a woman invested money in FCNR term deposits along with her husband. Both of them received separate tax notices from the 
Income Tax Department
 for unexplained income worth crores.
What the case is about
A woman, who originally hails from Beawar, and now resides in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE), decided to put money into investments in India. She along with her husband invested Rs 3.41 crore in two Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) term deposits.
The husband’s name appeared as the first holder of both deposits, with the woman listed as the second holder. The funds were accordingly transferred from Dubai to his Non-Resident External (NRE) account in a bank in India.
Also Read | 
Man skipped filing ITR and got tax notice so he declared Rs 12.9 lakh income; department imposed 200% penalty of Rs 3.99 lakh on taxable amount, but ITAT cancels it
The husband chose to hold the deposits in Japanese yen (JPY). The first deposit, worth 1.726 crore JPY, was opened on October 14, 2017, followed by a second deposit of 1.658 crore JPY on February 21, 2018, according to an ET report.
Despite jointly holding the FCNR deposits, the husband and his wife received separate income tax notices alleging unexplained money under Section 69A of the Income-tax Act.
This article focuses on the woman’s legal battle against the notice seeking to treat the deposits as unexplained money in her hands under Section 69A.
On September 22, 2026, the woman secured relief from the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) Jaipur.
Why did the woman win the case in ITAT?
ITAT Jaipur noted that the Income Tax Department had issued a notice under Section 133(6) to the concerned bank on November 9, 2022, seeking information about the transactions. In its response, the bank confirmed the transactions and provided details of the source of the funds.
The tribunal observed that the relevant information was therefore already available with the Income Tax Assessing Officer (AO). It also noted that the department had neither challenged the authenticity of the bank statements nor disputed the correctness of the assessment made in the woman’s husband's case.
Also Read | 
Man worked in South Korea and received salary in US dollars in NRE account, income tax department sent notice; ITAT Bangalore sets aside assessment and orders fresh review
ITAT Jaipur identified a significant error in the AO's assessment. The officer had mistakenly interpreted the amounts recorded in Japanese yen (JPY) as figures in Indian rupees.
Pointing out the discrepancy, the tribunal said the combined principal of the two deposits was JPY 3.384 crore, comprising JPY 1.726 crore and JPY 1.658 crore. However, the equivalent amount invested in Indian currency was Rs 2 crore. The addition of Rs 3.41 crore made by the AO did not correspond to any amount in rupees found in the woman’s possession.
The tribunal examined the bank statements and found that both FCNR deposits had been funded through debits from a jointly held NRE savings account. Before each debit, the account had received a credit of Rs 1 crore through the banking channel. The transaction narration carried the name of the woman’s husband and the first holder of the deposits.
The ITAT Jaipur said: “The immediate source is thus identified from the bank’s own record and points to the first holder. The Income Tax Department has not alleged, much less shown, that these funds arose from any source in India.”
The tribunal explained that Section 69A applies when a person is found to own money but fails to provide an explanation, or offers an explanation that is not satisfactory, regarding its nature and source.
Also Read | 
Man had Rs 2 crore bank deposit and didn’t file ITR, faced Rs 2.51 crore tax addition; ITAT Chennai quashes reassessment after Income Tax Department missed 6-year deadline by 5 days
In this case, however, the woman was the second holder of the FCNR deposits, while her husband was the first holder. Since the source of the money in the deposits had been explained by her husband, the tribunal found that the same funds could not be treated as unexplained money in the hands of the woman merely because she was the second holder.
ITAT Jaipur also considered the discrepancy in the records concerning the woman’s residential status. The CIT(A) had recorded her status as a non-resident, which was consistent with her Dubai address and the NRE and FCNR accounts reflected in the bank statements.
However, the AO's assessment order classified her as a resident without recording any finding to support that conclusion. The tribunal therefore treated the woman as a non-resident.
Under Section 5(2) of the Income-tax Act, income earned by a non-resident is taxable in India only if it is received or deemed to be received in India, or accrues or arises, or is deemed to accrue or arise, in the country. ITAT Jaipur observed that the department had not identified any income meeting these conditions in the woman’s case.
Rahul Jain, Partner at Khaitan & Co, explained to ET that the Indian tax liability of a non-resident Indian (NRI) generally extends only to income earned in India or received in the country. However, interest earned by a non-resident on funds held in an NRE account with an Indian bank is specifically exempt from Indian income tax. The principal amount deposited in an NRE account is also generally not taxable in India.
In this case, the tax authorities treated the entire amount held in the NRE account, covering both the principal and interest, as unexplained money and sought to tax it under Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
Also Read | 
Sisters sought share in parents’ properties under Hindu Succession law; Madras HC rules for brother over mother’s land on ouster, father’s estate over missing parties
Section 69A deals with money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable articles owned by a taxpayer for which the person either fails to explain the nature and source of acquisition or provides an explanation that the tax authorities do not find satisfactory.
During the appeal, the woman explained that her husband was the first holder of the disputed FCNR deposits and that the money had come from another jointly held NRE account with the same bank. She also submitted the relevant bank statements to support her explanation.
Another significant factor was that the same jurisdictional tax officer had examined her husband's explanation concerning the very same deposits and accepted it. Taking these circumstances into account, the CIT(A) ruled in the woman’s favour and deleted the additions made by the tax officer.
The matter subsequently came before the ITAT Jaipur, which observed that the tax authorities had not challenged the authenticity of the bank statements submitted by the woman.
ITAT Jaipur consequently upheld the CIT(A)'s order in her favour, confirming the deletion of the tax addition relating to the alleged unexplained money.

stories.headline: 'You have to wait': Iyer explains why Sooryavanshi missed all 5 T20Is
stories.deck: India captain Shreyas Iyer urged Vaibhav Sooryavanshi to remain patient and trust his process despite missing the entire West Indies T20I series. Iyer praised consistent openers Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma. Reflecting on India's 2-2 series draw, he blamed inconsistent bowling for missed opportunities and praised West Indies captain Shai Hope, who won Player of the Series.
stories.bodyText:
India captain 
Shreyas Iyer
 has backed young batter Vaibhav Sooryavanshi to remain patient and continue working on his game despite not getting a chance to play in the five-match T20I series against the West Indies. The series ended in a 2-2 draw after the rain-hit fifth match in Bengaluru was abandoned.
Sooryavanshi did not play in any of the five matches. His last appearance for India was in the Asian Games final against Pakistan. In eight T20Is, the youngster has scored 246 runs at a strike rate of over 186, including two half-centuries.
India continued to rely on experienced openers Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma throughout the series. Samson scored 168 runs in five matches, while Abhishek added 145 runs. Both batters registered two half-centuries, making it difficult for Sooryavanshi to find a place in the playing eleven.
Iyer advises Sooryavanshi to stay patient
Speaking after the fifth T20I, Iyer explained that he has been encouraging Sooryavanshi to trust his preparation and stay relaxed instead of worrying about missing out on opportunities.
"I just keep telling him [Vaibhav Sooryavanshi], you will get your opportunities. 
If you are consistent with your process, mindset a bit light and not think too much about not getting an opportunity....you have to wait sometimes. We have two fantastic openers who've been consistent throughout," the skipper said.
Iyer reflects on India's performance
Iyer said India could have achieved a better series result if the bowlers had performed more effectively in the second and fourth matches, when they conceded more than 240 runs. Despite the bowling struggles, he praised the team's batting and acknowledged the West Indies' strong performances.
"Could have been a different [series scoreline] if we had bowled well in the 2nd and 4th game. Batting has been sensational, execution we fell short. Credit where due, they batted phenomenally well. Kudos to Shai Hope; he was superb. The ability to bounce back even after a loss [among the big plusses]. We were not able to be consistent throughout, so great learning. Even today, the way we went about our batting was outstanding.
 Gonna be a challenging series in New Zealand now," he signed off.
West Indies captain 
Shai Hope
 was named Player of the Series after scoring 261 runs in four innings, including two centuries and a half-century, at a strike rate above 190.
In the rain-shortened fifth match, India scored an entertaining total after being asked to bat first. Ishan Kishan smashed 30 runs off just 10 balls, while Naman Dhir remained unbeaten on 24 from six deliveries. West Indies bowlers Shamar Springer and Keemo Paul picked up two wickets each.

stories.headline: Chris Woakes autobiography: Former England seamer slams Rob Key over 'shabby' exit
stories.deck: Woakes, who played 217 international matches for England across formats, including 62 Tests, made his final red-ball appearance during the fifth Test against India at The Oval in August 2025. Despite dislocating his shoulder while fielding, he came out to bat in a bid to help his team.
stories.bodyText:
Former England fast bowler 
Chris Woakes
 has described the way he was told he was no longer part of England's plans as ‘cold’ and ‘shabby’, saying managing director Rob Key could have spoken to him privately before making the announcement public.
Woakes, who played 217 international matches for England across formats, including 62 Tests, made his final red-ball appearance during the fifth Test against India at The Oval in August 2025. Despite dislocating his shoulder while fielding, he came out to bat in a bid to help his team.
However, the effort did not earn him a place in England's Ashes squad. Woakes subsequently announced his immediate retirement from international cricket.
In his autobiography, The Wizard, Woakes reflected on how England moved on from him. While he accepted his omission from last year's Ashes squad and the end of his England contract, he was hurt by the way Key publicly announced that he was no longer in the team's plans.
“Chris Woakes isn’t in our plans," Key said, adding, “at all." Looking back at the comments, Woakes wrote, as cited by The Guardian: “That final bit felt a bit cold. 
A bit shabby, really."
Woakes stopped short of directly criticising Key, suggesting the words may not have been intended in the way they came across.
“I have always got on well with Rob and maybe those words slipped out, not necessarily how he meant them. But he could have easily had that conversation first with me, rather than the press," Woakes wrote.
The two have had little contact since the incident, Woakes added, while acknowledging that professional sport often leaves little room for loyalty.
“We have barely spoken since. He is a busy man and moved on to different things. I am sure at some point we will discuss it. But in any walk of professional sport there isn’t much loyalty because the game moves on," Woakes added.
England's Ashes campaign later ended in a 4-1 defeat to Australia.

stories.headline: DP World India Championship: Norgaard takes lead on a rain-hit opening day
stories.deck: The Dane shoots six-under-par 66; McKibbin, Detry and Chacarra tied for second spot; McIlroy in tied 13th place; Om Prakash best among the Indians
stories.bodyText:
Danish golfer Niklas Norgaard sprang a surprise to take the sole lead on the opening day of the DP World India Championship at the Delhi Golf Club on Thursday.
On a rain-affected day, nearly five hours of play were lost. Norgaard, however, navigated the challenging conditions well to card an impressive six-under-par 66 to climb to the top of the leaderboard.
Norgaard went for broke in the first hole. After a pinpoint tee shot, he followed up with an impressive approach and sank a six-foot putt to return an eagle. The 34-year-old, who started on the back nine, explained his aggressive approach. “I hit a five-iron off the tee. As I walked up, I thought I had played a little too conservatively before, so I wanted to just go for it.”
Norgaard finished the round with two straight birdies.
Fan favourite Rory McIlroy had an uneventful round, shooting a two-under-par 70 to lie tied 13th. The lengthy rain delay appeared to disrupt McIlroy’s rhythm. The Northern Irishman returned to his hotel during the break before making his way back to the course when the rain subsided.
“It took me a little while to get going again,” McIlroy said.
The six-time Major champion was not overly concerned about his position. “The leaders have not gotten too far ahead. There is a lot of golf left,” he added.
McIlroy’s chief rival in the Race to Dubai, Eugenio Chacarra, fared better, moving into a tied second place with a five-under-par 67.
Chacarra held the outright lead heading into the ninth and final hole, but a late bogey — caused by pulling his tee shot left into the unforgiving rough — derailed his charge.
Second in the Race to Dubai standings, the Spaniard is also managing pain after breaking a toe a couple of weeks ago. “I’m still taking some medicines, but I’m feeling better every day,” he said.
It was a great day for Om Prakash Chouhan, who carded a four-under-par 68 to emerge as the best-performing Indian. “I had just one simple plan today — do not miss the fairway,” the experienced professional said.
For the 12 players who did not get to tee off, a long day of 36 holes awaits on Friday.

stories.headline: Manasi-Thulasimathi make semis, assure India of para badminton medal
stories.deck: With both losing semifinalists assured of bronze, the victory guaranteed India a place on the podium
stories.bodyText:
Manasi Joshi and Thulasimathi Murugesan assured India of a medal for the second successive edition, securing a semifinal berth in women's doubles SL3-SU5 at the Asian Para Games here on Saturday (October 17, 2026).
The Indian duo, who had bagged a silver at the Hangzhou edition in 2023, defeated China's Yuemei Liu and Tongtong Li 21-10, 21-17 to register their second successive win and confirm a top-two finish in Group A with a match to spare.
With both losing semifinalists assured of bronze, the victory guaranteed India a place on the podium.
Joshi and Thulasimathi had earlier defeated Indonesia's Rahayu Warining and Qonitah Ikhtiar Syakuroh on Friday. They will face China's Yang Qiuxia and Xiao Zuxian in their final group match on Monday.
The SL3-SU5 doubles event is a combined standing category for players with lower- or upper-limb impairments.
Tokyo Paralympics champion Krishna Nagar also notched his second successive win in the men's singles SH6 group stage to secure a quarterfinal berth.
Nagar defeated Indonesia's Subhan 21-13, 21-15 to confirm a top-two finish in Group C, with one group match still to play. The SH6 category is for players of short stature.
India enjoyed several other wins across the singles events, with Paris Paralympics champion Nitesh Kumar and Tokyo Paralympics winner Pramod Bhagat faring strongly in men's singles SL3, a category for players with lower-limb impairments who compete standing up.
Nitesh defeated Thailand's Natthapol Chamnanwet 21-6, 21-7, while Bhagat beat China's Xiong Lichuan 21-17, 21-16.
Umesh Vikram Kumar also defeated the Philippines' Khian Kyle Urbano 21-10, 21-12.
In men's singles SL4, which features standing players with less severe lower-limb impairments, Naveen Sivakumar beat Indonesia's Hikmat Ramdani 21-12, 21-10, while Surya Kant Yadav defeated Japan's Koki Ogawa 21-6, 21-19.
Sukant Kadam overcame South Korea's Shin Kyung Hwan 21-17, 18-21, 21-9, and Abhijeet Sakhuja rallied to beat Thailand's Siripong Teamarrom 19-21, 21-16, 21-10.
In men's singles SU5, a category for standing players with upper-limb impairments, Ruthick Ragupathi defeated Japan's Wataru Kanai 21-12, 21-13, while Hardik Makkar beat Malaysia's Amyrul Yazid bin Ahmad Sibi 21-16, 16-21, 21-18.
India also recorded victories in the wheelchair categories.
In men's singles WH1, for players with greater impairment affecting their trunk and lower limbs, Prem Kumar Ale overcame the UAE's Omair Younas 20-22, 21-9, 21-10.
In WH2, a category for wheelchair players with less severe impairment, Haris Mythili defeated Indonesia's Wiwin Andri 21-13, 21-17. Abu Hubaida, however, lost to Japan's Reo Oyama 13-21, 11-21.
In men's singles SH6, alongside Nagar's win, Sivarajan Solaimalai defeated Hong Kong's Wong Chun Yim 21-13, 21-14. Sudarsan Muthusamy, however, went down to Hong Kong's Chu Man Kai 8-21, 6-21.
In the women's events, Nithya Sre Sumathy Sivan beat China's Lin Shuangbao 21-18, 21-13 in singles SH6, while Thulasimathi Murugesan registered a dominant 21-2, 21-2 victory over Brunei's Zainab Mohamed in SU5. Manisha Ramadass also defeated compatriot Shanthiya Vishwanathan 21-8, 21-15 in the same category.
However India also endured setbacks in women's singles SL3, which features standing players with lower-limb impairments.
Joshi lost to Japan's Shino Kawai 3-21, 3-21, Sanjana Kumari went down to Indonesia's Qonitah Ikhtiar Syakuroh 13-21, 6-21, and Neeraj was beaten by China's Xiao Zuxian 5-21, 10-21.
Mandeep Kaur also lost to Malaysia's Siti Maisarah B. Mat Lawani 5-21, 13-21.
In women's singles SL4, Kanak Singh Jadaun suffered a 4-21, 3-21 defeat against China's Huang Zixuan, while Pallavi Kaluvehalli lost 13-21, 14-21 to China's Yang Fan in wheelchair singles WH1.
India also had mixed fortunes in the doubles events.
In men's doubles SL3-SU5, Surya Kant and Naveen Sivakumar defeated China's Mingpan Li and Lichuan Xiong 21-7, 21-19.
Sukant Kadam and Bhagat lost to South Korea's Shin Kyung Hwan and Cho Nadan 21-18, 19-21, 11-21, while Umesh Vikram Kumar and Rakesh Pandey went down to Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan and Hikmat Ramdani 14-21, 10-21.
In women's doubles SL3-SU5, Mandeep Kaur and Shanthiya Vishwanathan lost 11-21, 12-21 to China's Hefang Cheng and Zixuan Huang.
In mixed doubles WH1-WH2, Alphia James and Prem Kumar Ale defeated Chinese Taipei's I-Chen Yang and Yu-Yu Ong 21-9, 21-17. However, in mixed doubles SL3-SU5, Manisha Ramadass and Pramod Bhagat lost 19-21, 16-21 to Indonesia's Leani Ratri Oktila and Hikmat Ramdani, while Ruthick Ragupathi and Joshi were beaten 10-21, 17-21 by China's Mingpan Li and Zuxian Xiao.
Nagar and Nithya Sre Sumathy Sivan also went down 6-21, 10-21 to China's Naili Lin and Fengmei Li in mixed doubles SH6.

briefs.headline: PGTI plans to hike prize money in events next season: CEO Johl
briefs.bodyText:
The Professional Golf Tour of India (PGTI) plans to increase the prize money in its events next season, PGTI CEO Amandeep Johl said.
“We are going to switch from having the week-in-week-out tournaments. We will have the smaller tournaments in ‘B’ cities. We want to have bigger tournaments - ₹1.5 to ₹2 crore prize money upwards. The plan is to upgrade the existing tournaments,” Johl said on the sidelines of the DP World India Championship here on Thursday.
“We want to make them higher prize money tournaments, with more world-ranking points, and then provide an opportunity to the youngsters who miss out on qualifying school,” Johl said.
Johl explained that two ADT events, set to be held in February, have nearly been finalised.
The PGTI will do well to follow the BCCI model when it comes to attracting sponsors, Johl said. “Brands make an organisation. I’m only following the BCCI model. All the BCCI presidents brought in the big brands. We do not need to reinvent the wheel, just copy them. The money will follow, and the game will grow,” Johl said.

briefs.headline: Hope is doing well without taking much risk: Samson
briefs.deck: While he felt stiff chases often render anchors obsolete, Samson lauded Hope for going against the grain and marshalling the Windies with big scores
briefs.bodyText:
Sanju Samson single-handedly took over the PowerPlay as India stared at a daunting 248-run chase against the West Indies here.
He raced to a 20-ball half-century and looked primed to repeat the heroics at this venue from two years ago, when his century saw India fall just three short of the 300-run mark. But West Indies’ disciplined bowling did the job after Shai Hope’s unbeaten ton laid the foundation for the 24-run win at the Rajiv Gandhi International Stadium.
After a string of dismissals left India in troubled waters, a resurgence from local boys Tilak Varma and Nitish Kumar gave the home team hope before things eventually fell apart. “When Tilak and Nitish were batting, we were still in the game. That is a great thing to have even after losing five wickets... having that kind of control, two young cricketers taking on the pressure and taking on the West Indian bowling line-up,” Samson said after the fourth T20I.
The India opener rued that his own enterprising knock did not come in a winning cause. “I am actually a bit gutted. I definitely wanted to be on the winning side. When you are chasing a score like that, there are no second thoughts — you just have to back your instincts, power game, and that is what I did. So I really enjoyed the knock, but I would have liked to be on the winning side.”
While he felt stiff chases often render anchors obsolete, Samson lauded Hope for going against the grain and marshalling the Windies with big scores. “Hope is playing really well. We need to respect what he has been doing. He has been playing some really good cricketing shots, not taking that much risk, so he is respecting the bowlers as well.”

briefs.headline: Bowlers shouldn’t be too hard on themselves on bad days: Paul
briefs.deck: “We have some pretty long team bowling meetings. So we don’t take that (success with the ball) for granted. I knew what I wanted to do, I knew what my field setting was, and I knew my plan,” Keemo Paul said
briefs.bodyText:
At the Rajiv Gandhi International Cricket Stadium, a 10-over-old ball tends to stick in the surface, fertile ground for a clever bowler to deploy his variations and potentially change the face of the game. For West Indies, in its series-levelling win here on Wednesday, Keemo Paul was that man.
‘Execute or be executed,’ were his famous words to the Windies during the India series and he did just that. In his sensational five-wicket haul in the fourth T20I, Paul first removed a marauding Sanju Samson and Ishan Kishan in the span of four balls, using his pace to cramp the batter and drawing out edges before snapping up the key scalp of Nitish Kumar in the 19th to effectively snuff India’s hopes of an unlikely win.
He dismissed Prince Yadav and Axar Patel to get to the milestone a few deliveries later, becoming the first West Indian bowler to register multiple fifers in T20Is. He also became just the second man to claim a fifer against India in the format, following compatriot Obed McCoy (six for 17 in Basseterre, 2022).
“We have some pretty long team bowling meetings. So we don’t take that (success with the ball) for granted. I knew what I wanted to do, I knew what my field setting was, and I knew my plan,” he said, adding, “Obviously, I won’t share my plan (with you), but I think I executed pretty well tonight.”
A lack of dew in the second innings worked right into the visitors’ plans, Paul acknowledged.
“From the batsmen’s perspective, after the first five overs, the message we got was it was a pretty good wicket. One or two balls were gripping, but other than that, it was pretty good. Normally, we weren’t getting any grip, but it actually worked here. The game plan was to stick bowling into the wicket as long as possible.”
The 28-year-old, whose promising career has seen its share of injury interruptions, also declared that bowlers shouldn’t be too hard on themselves on bad days given the nature of wickets the format now gets.
“The margin for error is very, very thin. It all comes down to execution. It’s just about one day at a time. It’s all about the process. Once you try to stick to the team plan as much as possible, I don’t think the (coaching) staff would have a problem (if it doesn’t work out in the end).”

briefs.headline: Ranji Trophy: Batting woes continue to plague Tamil Nadu
briefs.deck: The performance of the pacers against Rajasthan in the opener was encouraging
briefs.bodyText:
Tamil Nadu’s Ranji Trophy opener against Rajasthan, where it conceded an 89-run first-innings lead, offered both familiar batting concerns and reasons for optimism in the pace department.
Tamil Nadu folded up for 274 in reply to Rajasthan’s 363. It needs its established batters to shoulder greater responsibility.
N. Jagadeesan (55) and Pradosh Ranjan Paul (58) batted together for nearly half of the second day, but neither converted his half-century into a substantial score. Jagadeesan, in particular, will rue his dismissal, holing out to long-off off left-arm spinner Kukna Ajay Singh.
Andre Siddarth has been a source of encouragement for Tamil Nadu across three consecutive seasons. Known for his positive intent, the 20-year-old has shown he can play both counter-attacking and attritional innings, as his 192-ball 81 demonstrated. With a First Class average of 54.45, he has made a compelling case for consideration higher up the order.
The side lost its last five wickets for 10 runs. The lower-order’s lack of application, as pointed out by skipper Sai Kishore, has been a recurring problem in recent seasons.
Mumbai, for instance, has benefited from the batting depth provided by Shams Mulani, Tanush Kotian, Shardul Thakur, and even Tushar Deshpande. Tamil Nadu needs similar contributions from its lower-order. Instead, Washington Sundar was left stranded as wickets fell at the other end.
On an initially placid surface, Saravana Kumar and D. Deepesh were workhorse-like. The 37-year-old Saravana Kumar, playing only his third Ranji match, claimed three of the four wickets on the opening day and finished with figures of three for 68 in the first essay. He removed two well-set batters, Sumit Godara (49) and Rohan Rajbar (95), breaking both of Rajasthan’s century partnerships.
Wicketless for 18.5 overs, debutant Deepesh persisted with the short ball and claimed three wickets in his next eight deliveries (three for 89), triggering a collapse. His pace and bounce are valuable assets, while Gurjapneet Singh’s return should make the pace attack more potent.

briefs.headline: Want to still take a crack at the 400m world record:Miller-Uibo
briefs.bodyText:
The mention of Shaunae Miller-Uibo elicits memories of her famous dive across the finish line to win gold in the women’s 400m at the 2016 Rio Olympics. It helped the Bahamian track and field sprinter, who specialises in the 200m and 400m, pip Allyson Felix by 0.07 seconds for the yellow metal.
A decade has passed, but Miller-Uibo, who is in India for the first time in her capacity as an international ambassador for Sunday’s Vedanta Delhi Half Marathon, remembers the moment vividly.
“I remember that when I had covered the first 100m, I felt very great. But with 50m to go, I did not have anything left to give. I heard everyone’s footsteps around me. I saw Allyson in my (peripheral) view and that is what had me leaning towards the line,” she took a trip down memory lane at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium here on Thursday evening.
She went on to defend her gold medal five years later at the Tokyo Olympics. She also won gold at the 2022 Eugene World Championships. However, the 32-year-old isn’t done yet, never mind that she is now the mother of two children.
With the World Championships slated for 2027 followed by the 2028 LA Olympics, Miller-Uibo, whose personal best in 400m is 48.36 seconds, is still targeting the world record. That belongs to East Germany’s Marita Koch, who was timed at 47.60s in 1985. In the 200m, Miller-Uibo’s personal best is 21.74 seconds while Florence Griffith-Joyner (21.34s) holds the world record.
“I had two babies. One in 2023 and another in 2025. I have been building back up ever since. This season went really well for me. I was trying to shake off the rust. It is about setting new goals for myself. I would like to give a crack at the world record. I feel I am more than capable of doing it,” she asserted.

briefs.headline: DP World India Championship: McIlroy-Reed mend fences after rift
briefs.deck: Earlier this year, Reed quit LIV Golf, which perhaps helped clear the way for the two golf giants to find common ground
briefs.bodyText:
The tense relationship between Rory McIlroy and Patrick Reed appeared to ease as the two golfers exchanged pleasantries at the Delhi Golf Club during the DP World India Championship here.
The rift began a few years ago when Reed moved to LIV Golf while McIlroy remained fiercely loyal to the PGA Tour.
Things got ugly, at least by genteel golf standards, at the 2023 Hero Dubai Desert Classic, when McIlroy appeared to ignore Reed at the practice range. Reed responded by flicking a LIV-branded tee towards McIlroy.
McIlroy later revealed that he was miffed at being served a subpoena by Reed’s lawyer on Christmas Eve, some months earlier.
Speaking after carding a two-under-par first round on Thursday, McIlroy suggested that it was best to leave the past behind. “There are no lawsuits anymore, so that helps (laughs),” he said.
The Northern Irishman, who is currently battling Reed in the Race to Dubai, added that he respected the way his rival had returned to the fold. Earlier this year, Reed quit LIV Golf, which perhaps helped clear the way for the two golf giants to find common ground.
“Patrick has put his head down and let the clubs do the talking. Patrick and I have had some battles over the years, and I respect him as a competitor. The character he has shown in coming back to the PGA Tour has meant a lot to the guys on the Tour. He has done it the right way. That speaks a lot about who he is and how he has evolved,” McIlroy said.

briefs.headline: Umar hopes to prove a point against Vidarbha
briefs.deck: The Jammu and Kashmir was ‘rested’ for the Ranji Trophy opener against Madhya Pradesh
briefs.bodyText:
With a point to prove after being ‘rested’ for J&K’s Ranji Trophy opener, Umar Nazir found an unlikely mentor in BCCI president Mithun Manhas.
During breaks in the game against Madhya Pradesh, Manhas watched the tall pacer bowl in the nets, even placing a stump behind him to check his landing and guard against overstepping. Manhas’ long association with J&K brought out the cricketer in him as he stepped in to help Umar fine-tune his run-up.
Umar, who returned a match haul of five for 157 in the Irani Cup earlier this month, is set to return against Vidarbha later this week, with Auqib Nabi joining the India-A squad for the tour of New Zealand.
J&K will need the 32-year-old to step up after struggling to make inroads at crucial moments against MP. The batting, too, failed to show the resolve needed as the defending champion escaped with a draw.
Captain Paras Dogra acknowledged that the team had fallen short in both departments. With Yudhvir Singh unfit, J&K’s options have been limited, while Nasir Lone bowled just 16 overs against MP.
The bigger concern remains the batting. J&K has struggled to build partnerships, leaving the middle-order with too much to do. Dogra believes the openers must lead the recovery and provide a platform for the rest.
“Our batters have not been up to the mark and have failed to build partnerships. The bowlers have been performing fairly well, both in the Irani Cup and in the Ranji opener,” he told The Hindu. “We hope Umar will be fresh and ready for the next game.”
For Umar, the Vidarbha fixture offers a chance to turn disappointment into opportunity. He will be keen to exploit the conditions and add bite to an attack that lacked consistency against MP.
